prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. I was trudging along a muddy path in a column of downcast men on the blackened outskirts of New York, the twilight dingy and ruined, the future without hope as we marched along in our soiled, proletarian rags. To my left was Mayakovsky, head shaved, and next to him his friend with gray beard and dark cap. "You've got to admit," Mayakovsky was saying, "that this is a pretty good way to write a poem." "Yes," I said, "the momentum is sustained by our walking forward, the desolate landscape seeps into every word, and you're free to say anything you want." "That's because we're inside the poem," he said, "not outside." Puddles of oily water gleamed dully beneath the low clouds. "That's why my poems were so big: there's more room inside." The hard line of his jaw flexed and the men dispersed. I followed his friend behind a wall to hear the poem go on in the lecture the friend was giving on history, but no, the real poem had finished. I went back to the spot where the poem had finished. Vladimir had left the poem.

outputs.L2:
Fine, I confess: none of it was real—it came to me in a dream last night. I found myself moving laboriously down a mud-covered road among a line of dejected men. We were passing through New York’s scorched outer districts beneath a grim, decaying dusk, dressed in filthy workers’ clothing and advancing toward a hopeless future.

Mayakovsky walked on my left, his scalp bare. Beside him was his companion, who wore a dark cap and had a graying beard.

“You have to agree,” Mayakovsky remarked, “this is quite an effective method for composing a poem.”

“I do,” I replied. “Our steady movement keeps it driving onward, the bleak surroundings penetrate the language, and nothing restricts what you can say.”

“That’s because we’re within the poem rather than observing it from beyond,” he answered.

Under the low-hanging sky, pools coated with oil gave off a muted shine.

“And that,” he continued, “is why my poems were enormous: their interiors had greater space.”

His sharply defined jaw tightened, and the group of men scattered. Hoping the poem would continue, I trailed his friend behind a wall and listened as he delivered a talk about history. But I was mistaken—the true poem had already ended.

I returned to the place where it had stopped. Vladimir was no longer inside the poem.
outputs.L3: The narrator eventually reveals that the bleak procession through New York has been a dream. Within this dream, he marches beside the poet Vladimir Mayakovsky through a desolate landscape marked by ruin and emptiness. As they walk, Mayakovsky explains that their continued movement sustains the poem’s momentum: the act of crossing the landscape keeps the verse alive and gives it complete freedom of expression. He adds that his poems could become so expansive because their participants existed “inside” them, directly experiencing the poem rather than standing outside it as detached observers. The poem finally comes to an end when the men disperse and Mayakovsky departs. Although the narrator tries to follow him and discover how the poem might continue, he is unable to do so, and the dreamlike journey concludes with Mayakovsky’s disappearance.
outputs.L4:
The narrator recounts a bleak dream in which he travels beside the Russian poet Vladimir Mayakovsky. Together they march through a devastated landscape, crossing empty, ruined spaces that seem to stretch without limit. The journey is grim, yet it also possesses a strange energy: as long as the two figures continue moving, the dream—and the poem that contains it—keeps unfolding. Their steady progress through the wasteland gives the experience direction and momentum, even though no clear destination is in sight.

During the march, the narrator and Mayakovsky speak about their situation and gradually recognize that they are “inside” a poem. This realization turns the dream into a reflection on poetic composition. The landscape is not merely a backdrop but part of the poem’s creative machinery. Its vastness allows the imagination to roam, while the act of walking supplies rhythm, continuity, and forward motion. Because the speakers are immersed in the poem rather than observing it from outside, they experience poetry as a space that can be entered, crossed, and inhabited.

Mayakovsky’s presence reinforces the poem’s sense of scale and freedom. Associated with bold language, public speech, and revolutionary ambition, he becomes both a companion and a guide through this imaginative territory. The ruined world around the two poets may suggest historical catastrophe, political disappointment, or personal desolation, but it also creates an open field in which the poem can expand. Movement through that field frees the writing from ordinary limits: each new step can generate another image, thought, or exchange.

The dream therefore presents composition as an immersive journey. A poem gathers force when its speaker enters fully into its setting and allows images, rhythm, and movement to carry the writing forward. Yet this momentum is fragile. When Mayakovsky suddenly leaves, the journey cannot continue. His departure does not lead to a gradual conclusion or a carefully prepared resolution; instead, it breaks the imaginative spell on which the poem depends.

The ending is consequently abrupt and irreversible. Once the companion who sustained the dialogue and the movement has vanished, the narrator cannot simply recover the lost momentum. The poetic world closes as suddenly as a dream ends upon waking. Mayakovsky’s departure thus marks not only the loss of a fellow traveler but also the termination of the creative process itself. The poem ends because the conditions that made it possible—shared movement, immersion, and imaginative companionship—have disappeared.

# All About New York

New York is a city for all—dreamers, travelers, artists, and entrepreneurs. From the bright lights of Times Square to the peaceful paths of Central Park, every neighborhood offers something new to discover. Visitors can explore world-famous museums, enjoy food from across the globe, and admire the iconic skyline. With its energy, diversity, and endless possibilities, New York truly has something for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about dreaming that you walk through a ruined New York with Vladimir Mayakovsky while discussing what it means to be “inside” a poem.
counterfactuals.output:
I dream New York has been left too long in the rain. The towers lean like wet books; avenues unspool into rivers of black glass. In Times Square, the dead billboards whisper their last commands to pigeons.

Mayakovsky walks beside me in a yellow shirt bright enough to insult the ruins. He is enormous. Each step stamps an exclamation mark into the asphalt.

“To be inside a poem,” he says, “is not to live in a house.”

A subway entrance yawns at our feet. From below comes the sound of a century changing trains.

“Then what is it?” I ask.

He kicks a taxi rusting beneath a pear tree. The taxi rings like a bell.

“It is to be inside the blow that breaks the house.”

We cross Broadway, where the traffic lights have grown roots. Red, yellow, green apples hang from their wires. Mayakovsky plucks the red one and bites it; sirens pour from his mouth and circle the moon.

I tell him I have always imagined a poem as a room: four walls of language, one locked door, a window opening onto the impossible.

“Too comfortable,” he says. “Where is the staircase that climbs through your chest? Where is the landlord demanding your name?”

At Forty-Second Street, the lions from the library are drinking from a burst hydrant. Their stone tongues have become soft and pink. Behind them, books stagger down the steps, shedding pages like frightened birds. One opens at my feet. Inside is the street we are standing on. Inside that street, we stand again, smaller, walking past the same ruined theaters, having the same conversation. Mayakovsky bends over the page and shouts to his miniature self, but the smaller poet only looks up and puts a finger to his lips.

“Perhaps,” I say, “being inside a poem means the poem is larger than you.”

“Everything is larger than you,” he replies. “Hunger. History. A woman leaving the room.”

The Empire State Building has fallen across the island like a colossal tuning fork. Wind moves through it, and Manhattan hums. Windows tremble loose from the air. In each window I see another dreamer crossing another city with another impossible companion: Dante in Los Angeles, Sappho in Shanghai, a child walking through Kyiv with the ghost of a future poet.

Mayakovsky presses his ear to the pavement.

“The poem is coming,” he says.

“From where?”

“From underneath what you meant.”

Then the city folds. The Hudson rises vertically, a blue wall crowded with ferries. Central Park closes like a green mouth. Skyscrapers become letters; streets become spaces between them. We are no longer walking through New York but through a sentence spelling New York, and every ruined building is a word that has survived its meaning.

I feel punctuation gathering in the sky.

Mayakovsky stops at the edge of dawn. His yellow shirt is now the only sun.

“To be inside a poem,” he says, softer than rubble settling, “is to discover there is no outside. Only the white margin pretending not to burn.”

He steps into a broken window and vanishes.

I wake with Manhattan in my mouth—iron, rain, one red apple—and somewhere below my bed a subway keeps arriving, its doors opening and opening onto the unwritten.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short literary dream narrative in the first person, featuring Mayakovsky, a muddy proletarian procession, and a metafictional conversation about poetic form.
counterfactuals.output:
I dreamed Mayakovsky knocked on my window with a red umbrella.

Outside, a proletarian procession trudged through mud thick as printer’s ink. Factory women carried banners whose slogans kept revising themselves; machinists beat time on dented pails. Each step printed a dark exclamation point upon the street.

“Come,” Mayakovsky commanded. His voice shook rain from the gutters.

I joined him. We marched beside a horse wearing spectacles. Somewhere an accordion attempted the Internationale and forgot the middle.

“Your dream lacks structure,” Mayakovsky said.

“It’s a prose poem,” I protested.

“Then why does it walk in sentences?”

“Because lines would sink in this mud.”

He frowned and pulled a ladder from his coat. “A poem must climb—even when history kneels.”

“But who is speaking now?” I asked. “You, or my idea of you?”

He stopped. The entire procession stopped behind him, though the accordion continued alone.

“That,” he said, pointing at me, “is the only honest line you’ve written.”

Then he broke the sky into narrow stanzas. Dawn showed between them like blank paper. The workers climbed upward, boots dripping commas, banners snapping at the margins.

I tried to follow, but woke with mud between my toes and a single red feather on my pillow.

It may have been from the umbrella.

Or from the poem, escaping.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine an encounter between the narrator and Vladimir Mayakovsky in a bleak post-apocalyptic landscape. Let their physical movement through the scene become a metaphor for how poetry sustains momentum, and end with Mayakovsky leaving the poem.
counterfactuals.output:
The road had forgotten what it was for.

It ran beneath a sky the color of an extinguished screen, past apartment blocks opened like books in the rain. Elevators hung in their shafts. Traffic lights blinked red to no one. I walked because stopping felt too much like agreeing with the world.

Then Mayakovsky stepped from the husk of a tram.

He was immense—coat flapping, jaw set against the wind, a yellow scarf burning at his throat. He carried no luggage except his voice.

“Why do you drag your feet?” he demanded.

“There’s nowhere left to go.”

“Then go there loudly.”

We crossed the avenue. Glass crackled under our boots, keeping time. At each intersection he shouted a word—*Bread!* *Comrade!* *Sun!*—and the ruined facades threw it back, altered but alive. I answered with smaller words. *Still.* *Here.* *Yes.*

Soon our steps became lines.

His were long, vaulting over craters and overturned buses. Mine limped after, breaking where the ground broke, learning that a pause was not the same as an ending. When the wind rose, we leaned into it like a stanza leaning into silence. When ash erased our footprints, we made new ones.

“Poetry,” he said, climbing the collapsed ribs of a bridge, “is not a shelter.”

Below us, the river pushed black ice toward the sea.

“No,” I said. “It’s the walking.”

He looked at me then—not kindly, but with the fierce approval of a match recognizing fire.

We descended the far side. With every step the city thinned: tower, wall, doorway, stone. At last there was only a white plain and the horizon’s narrow seam.

Mayakovsky stopped.

I took another step.

Then another.

Behind me, paper rustled. I turned and saw him at the edge of the final line, removing his scarf, his coat, his thunderous name. One by one he dropped them into the snow.

He raised a hand—not farewell, exactly, but punctuation.

Then Vladimir Mayakovsky stepped beyond the margin and left the poem.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a paragraph of experimental prose that begins as a confession that the events were only a dream. Use dingy twilight, oily puddles, marching workers, a ruined New York, and dialogue about why Mayakovsky’s poems were so large.
counterfactuals.output: I confess: it was only a dream. In the dingy twilight, ruined New York leaned sideways into oily puddles, every shattered window repeating a different, bruised moon, while workers marched down Broadway with iron lunchboxes beating against their knees like metronomes. “Why were Mayakovsky’s poems so large?” you asked from beneath a newspaper hat. “Because whispers could not cross the factories,” I said, though the factories were hollow, though the workers had no faces, though each enormous word was already climbing the walls in red boots. MAY—A—KOV—SKY, the syllables strode ahead of us, taller than the Chrysler Building’s broken needle, and the puddles applauded with black hands. Then dawn, that bad foreman, blew its whistle; the marchers folded into smoke, Manhattan sank through the mattress, and I woke with a mouth full of type.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a melancholic, self-referential prose poem in which the speaker trudges beside Mayakovsky and his gray-bearded friend. Blur the boundaries among dream, poem, lecture, and history, concluding with the realization that the real poem has ended.
counterfactuals.output:
I trudged beside Mayakovsky through a snow that seemed less weather than punctuation. His coat was open, as though he had quarreled with winter and refused to acknowledge its reply. On his other side walked his gray-bearded friend, whose name I had forgotten—or had never been told—carrying under one arm a folder of yellow lectures and under the other the exhausted century.

We were late for a dream.

Mayakovsky spoke in red staircases. Each sentence climbed loudly, then broke beneath him. The old man answered with dates: 1905, 1917, tomorrow. Whenever he said tomorrow, the snow deepened. I wanted to ask where we were going, but saw that the question had already been written several lines ahead, where a black bridge bent over a frozen river.

Below us, history rehearsed its drowning. Crowds moved under the ice, lifting banners whose words had blurred into water. A professor’s voice explained their failure from somewhere above the clouds. I took notes, though my notebook was this paragraph and my hand was only a metaphor the lecturer would later dispute.

“Do not confuse the poem with what happened,” said the gray-bearded friend.

“Do not confuse what happened with what survives,” Mayakovsky shouted.

Then the bridge became a corridor, the corridor a classroom, and the snow tapped softly at the windows like students who had arrived after the revolution. Mayakovsky stood at the lectern. His friend erased the future from the board. I sat among the dead, listening to myself describe our walk in the past tense.

At some point I awoke, but waking merely changed the lighting. The lecture continued inside the dream; the dream continued inside this sentence. Mayakovsky was suddenly far ahead, enormous and solitary, dragging his shadow like a torn flag. The old man had vanished. In his place trudged a comma, gray-bearded and patient, asking me not to stop.

But the street narrowed to a margin. The century closed its folder. Snow covered the footprints, then the footnotes, then the voice that had mistaken remembering for rescue.

Only then did I understand: we had not been walking through the poem. We had been walking away from it.

The real poem had ended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
